8.title: the man who argued with God about Sodom
8.hook: the man who argued with God about Sodom
8.howItsDone: Jews read Abraham's argument over Sodom in the Torah portion Vayera each autumn, and the Jewish tradition of questioning and arguing, with God and with one another, runs through the Psalms, Job and the Talmud's recorded debates.

segments.voice: Yesterday: machloket, rabbis arguing for the sake of heaven. Your line was argue to learn, not to win. Week two starts with a bigger argument. Day eight.
screen: `ARGUE TO LEARN, NOT TO WIN.` → `WEEK TWO.`

segments.voice: An old man is sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day. Three visitors arrive, he feeds them, and as they leave, God tells him something. The cities of the plain, Sodom and Gomorrah, have done terrible things, and God is going to see about them. He could bow, or nod, or quietly go back inside. He doesn't. The text says he comes closer. And then he starts to argue. With God. Today: an argument with God, and the man who made it.
screen: `A TENT IN THE HEAT OF THE DAY.` → `GOD SPEAKS OF SODOM.` → `ABRAHAM COMES CLOSER.`

segments.voice: Abraham. Born Abram, the text says, and renamed when God promised he'd be the father of many nations. Jews call him Avraham avinu, Abraham our father. And here, he bargains. What if there are fifty good people in the city? Will you sweep them away with the rest? Then comes the line at the center of the story: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" That takes nerve. He's holding God to God's own standard. And God answers: for fifty, I'll spare it. So Abraham keeps going. Forty-five? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? Each time he gets more polite, and more stubborn. He calls himself "but dust and ashes," and still doesn't back down. He stops at ten. Why ten? The text doesn't say. Some teachers note that ten is the smallest number that makes a community. In the end, ten good people aren't found. But the argument is never scolded. God listens to every round. And Abraham isn't the last. Moses argues with God later. So does Job. The psalms complain out loud. There's a Hasidic story of a rabbi who put God on trial on behalf of his people. Arguing with God, in this tradition, isn't the opposite of faith. It's one of the ways faith talks.
screen: `ABRAM BECOMES ABRAHAM.` · `WHAT IF THERE ARE FIFTY?` · `FROM FIFTY DOWN TO TEN.` · `ARGUING IS HOW FAITH TALKS.` · then, large: `SHALL NOT THE JUDGE OF ALL THE EARTH DO JUSTLY?`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Bring to mind one thing that seems unfair to you right now, in your life or in the world. Don't smooth it over. Say it plainly, inside. If you pray, you can say it to God the way Abraham did: direct, respectful, and not backing down. If you don't, say it honestly to yourself.
Abraham. Father of many nations, who argued with God on behalf of strangers. Eighth word.
Your line: you're allowed to argue. Direct, respectful, and on behalf of someone else: that's how Abraham did it. Day eight.

9.title: wrestling all night, limping, renamed
9.carry: you'll limp and you'll be blessed
9.tomorrow: "we will do and we will hear"
9.howItsDone: Jews read Jacob's wrestling in the Torah portion Vayishlach each year; the name Israel, the people's name, comes from this story, and observant Jews still do not eat the sciatic nerve of an animal because of Jacob's hip.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abraham, bargaining with God from fifty down to ten. Your line was you're allowed to argue. Today, his grandson goes further. Day nine.

It's the night before the hardest meeting of his life. Twenty years ago Jacob cheated his twin brother Esau out of their father's blessing and ran. Now he's coming home, and Esau is on the road with four hundred men. Jacob sends his family across a river called the Jabbok and stays behind, alone, in the dark. And then, the text says, a man wrestles with him until the break of dawn. No name. No warning. No explanation. Just two bodies in the dirt all night long. Today: the wrestler, and the name the whole people still carries.
screen: `TWENTY YEARS AFTER THE LIE.` → `ALONE AT THE RIVER.` → `A MAN WRESTLES HIM TILL DAWN.`

segments.voice: Jacob. In Hebrew, Yaakov, from the word for heel, because he was born holding on to his twin brother's heel. He's been grabbing ever since. Who is he fighting? The text calls him a man. The prophet Hosea calls him an angel. Jacob himself names the place Peniel, the face of God, because he says he saw God face to face. One old midrash says it was Esau's angel. The Torah doesn't settle it, and maybe that's the point: some nights you can't tell who you're fighting. As dawn comes, the stranger can't win, so he touches Jacob's hip and wrenches it. And Jacob, hurt, still won't let go: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." The blessing is a new name. "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel; for thou hast striven with God and with men, and hast prevailed." Israel: one who wrestles with God. A whole people named not for someone who obeyed quietly, or never doubted, but for someone who fought all night and held on. And he doesn't walk away clean. The sun rises, and Jacob is limping. The Torah says that's why the children of Israel don't eat the sinew of the thigh, and observant Jews still don't. A food law that remembers an injury. He's hurt, and he's renamed, in the same morning.
screen: `YAAKOV — THE ONE WHO GRABS THE HEEL.` · `A MAN, AN ANGEL, OR GOD?` · `ISRAEL — WRESTLES WITH GOD.` · `THE BLESSING AND THE LIMP.` · then, large: `I WILL NOT LET THEE GO, EXCEPT THOU BLESS ME.`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Think of one thing you're wrestling with right now: a decision, a person, a question. Don't try to win it in the next minute. Just hold on to it, the way Jacob held on, and ask what blessing might be in it. If you pray, you can ask for that blessing.
Jacob. The heel-grabber who wrestled until dawn, came away limping, and was renamed Israel. Ninth word.
Your line: you'll limp and you'll be blessed. The mark and the new name came in the same morning. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 9 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "WE WILL DO AND WE WILL HEAR".`

10.title: "we will do and we will hear"
10.hook: "we will do and we will hear" — practice before belief
10.howItsDone: Jews celebrate the giving of the Torah at Sinai on the festival of Shavuot, seven weeks after Passover; some stay up all night studying Torah, and the Ten Commandments are read aloud in synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jacob, who wrestled till dawn and was renamed Israel. Your line was you'll limp and you'll be blessed. Today, his descendants, out of Egypt, at a mountain. Day ten.

Three months out of Egypt, a crowd of former slaves is camped at the foot of a mountain in the desert. They've been told to wash, to wait, to keep back from the slopes. On the third morning there's thunder, lightning, a thick cloud on the peak, and the sound of a horn growing louder and louder until the whole camp is shaking. Later, what this new life with God will ask is read out loud to them. And the people give an answer, all together, that the rabbis would keep coming back to. It's two words in Hebrew, and they're in the wrong order. Today: the mountain, and the answer.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN IN THE DESERT.` → `THUNDER, CLOUD, A HORN.` → `AN ANSWER IN THE WRONG ORDER.`

segments.voice: Sinai is the mountain where, in the Torah's story, God gives the Torah to Israel. Where exactly it stood is uncertain, and the text isn't interested in the map. What matters is what happens there. After the laws are read, the people say: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew: na'aseh v'nishma. We will do, and we will hear. Look at the order. The usual order runs the other way: explain it to me first, then I'll decide whether to do it. Here the doing comes first, and the understanding follows. The rabbis tell a story about that moment: when Israel put doing before hearing, a voice from heaven asked, who revealed to my children this secret that the angels use? Teachers hear in it practice before belief. You light the candles, as on day two, before you have a theory of candles. The meaning grows out of the doing. The rabbis also argued about that day, and they wrote the argument down. One teacher said the mountain was held over the people like a barrel, as if they had no real choice. Others answered that they accepted freely, and accepted again in later generations. Both readings are kept. And one more teaching: every Jewish soul, even of people not yet born, stood at Sinai, converts too. The whole people, past and future, at the foot of one mountain. Jews mark that day every year, at the festival of Shavuot.
screen: `THE MOUNTAIN WHERE TORAH IS GIVEN.` · `NA'ASEH V'NISHMA — DO, THEN HEAR.` · `THE SECRET THE ANGELS USE.` · `EVERY SOUL STOOD THERE.` · then, large: `WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Think of one good thing you've been putting off until you understand it better, or feel more ready. A call. An apology. A habit. Picture yourself doing it first, and letting the understanding come afterward.
Sinai. The mountain of the covenant, where the people answered: we will do, and we will hear. Tenth word.
Your line: do first. The understanding tends to arrive a little later. Day ten, done.

11.title: the oldest labor law
11.hook: the oldest labor law; a day the world can't have
11.howItsDone: Jews mark Shabbat from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall with candles, blessings over wine and bread, a family meal and synagogue; observant Jews refrain from the thirty-nine categories of work, while others keep it through the meal, rest and a slower day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sinai, and the answer we will do, and we will hear. Your line was do first. On day two you lit the candles; today, the day they open. Day eleven.

A phone on a Saturday looks like a phone on a Tuesday. Work email. The group chat. A sale that ends tonight. The world never really closes anymore. Now take a family that, every week, from Friday sunset until the stars come out on Saturday, lets none of that in. No office. No shopping. In some homes, not even a light switch. Not a holiday, not a sick day. Just the seventh day, arriving on schedule. Some people call it the oldest labor law there is. Today: the day the world can't have.
screen: `THE WORLD NEVER CLOSES.` → `A DAY IT CAN'T REACH.` → `THE SEVENTH DAY.`

segments.voice: Shabbat comes from a Hebrew root, shin, bet, tav, that means to stop. To cease. Not first to relax, or to worship: to stop. At the end of the creation story, even God stops, and the verb there comes from the same root. English borrowed the word as Sabbath. Then the rabbis asked a practical question: what counts as work? They listed thirty-nine kinds: planting, baking, writing, building, lighting a fire, and more, drawn from the work it took to build the tent for God in the desert. So work, on Shabbat, means making and changing things, not how tired you get. Now the part that earns the nickname. The rest day is commanded twice, and the second time it gives a different reason. Not creation. Egypt. You were slaves, so rest, "that thy man-servant and thy maid-servant may rest as well as thou." As well as you. Not after you. And the list of who rests keeps going: your children, the stranger in your town, even the ox and the donkey. A weekly day off, owed to everyone, written into an ancient law. Jews keep the day in different ways. Orthodox Jews keep the thirty-nine categories carefully: no driving, no cooking, no phones. Conservative, Reform and other Jews keep Shabbat in their own ways, through the candles, the meal, synagogue and a slower day, with each community drawing its own lines. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described Shabbat as a palace built in time rather than in space. You don't travel to it. It arrives, every week, wherever you are.
screen: `SHABBAT — TO STOP.` · `THIRTY-NINE KINDS OF WORK.` · `REST, BECAUSE YOU WERE SLAVES.` · `A PALACE IN TIME.` · then, large: `AS WELL AS THOU.`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Put one thing down with each breath. The thing you're working on. The thing you're worried about. The phone, if it's in your hand. For these few breaths, nothing is being made or fixed. That's the whole idea of Shabbat, very small.
Shabbat. To stop: the seventh day, Friday sunset to Saturday stars, a rest owed to everyone in the house. Eleventh word.
Your line: stop. it's already Friday. Rest isn't a prize for finishing; it's owed. Day eleven.

12.title: hello, goodbye, peace
12.hook: hello, goodbye, peace — and a fourth meaning: whole
12.howItsDone: Shalom is said as hello and goodbye, and Shabbat shalom on the Sabbath; the priestly blessing, which ends with a prayer for peace, is said in synagogue and in some homes by parents over their children on Friday night.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabbat, the day of stopping. Your line was stop. it's already Friday. Today, the word people say once the candles are lit: Shabbat shalom. Day twelve.

One word, three jobs. Someone walks in: shalom. Someone leaves: shalom. On a card, at the end of a letter, over a door: shalom, peace. Hello, goodbye, peace. The same word opens a conversation and closes it. But there's a fourth meaning hiding underneath the other three, and it's the one the rest of them grow from. Today, the wish folded inside the hello.
screen: `HELLO. GOODBYE. PEACE.` → `ONE WORD, THREE JOBS.` → `AND A FOURTH MEANING.`

segments.voice: Shalom is Hebrew, and it grows from a root of three letters, shin, lamed, mem, and the root's first sense isn't quiet. It's whole. Complete. Nothing missing. The same root gives shalem, whole, and a verb for paying back what you owe, so the account is square again. So peace, in this language, isn't only the absence of a fight. It's the presence of everything that should be there. A house with shalom has nothing broken in it. A body with shalom is well. In the Torah, when Jacob sends his son Joseph to check on his brothers, the Hebrew says, more or less: go and see the shalom of your brothers. How whole are they? The word runs all through Jewish prayer. The priestly blessing, said over congregations, and in some homes over the children on Friday night, ends with it: "and give thee peace." Peace is the last word. And an old psalm doesn't treat peace as something that just happens to you: "Seek peace, and pursue it." The rabbis noticed that verb. Other commandments, they taught, you do when the chance comes to you. Peace you go after. So when someone says shalom at a door, coming or going, underneath the hello is an old wish: may you be whole. May nothing be missing.
screen: `SH-L-M — WHOLE, COMPLETE.` · `SEE THE SHALOM OF YOUR BROTHERS.` · `THE BLESSING ENDS IN PEACE.` · `SEEK PEACE, AND PURSUE IT.` · then, large: `MAY NOTHING BE MISSING.`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Breathe slowly, and notice one place in you that feels not quite whole right now. Tired. Worried. Rushed. Don't fix it; just let it be noticed. On the last breath, if you want to, say the word, out loud or inside: shalom. Not to fix anything. Just to wish it whole.
Shalom. Hello, goodbye, peace, and underneath all three: whole, with nothing missing. Twelfth word.
Your line: be whole. It's the wish folded inside every hello and goodbye. That's day twelve.

13.title: six words
13.hook: six words; the sentence a Jew says with eyes covered
13.howItsDone: Jews traditionally say the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and again at bedtime, covering the eyes with the right hand for the first line; some parents say it with their children as they fall asleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shalom, and underneath the hello, whole. Your line was be whole. Today, the words rolled up inside the mezuzah from day one. Day thirteen.

A synagogue on an ordinary morning. People are reading, murmuring, some standing, some swaying. Then, at one moment, many of them do the same small thing. They raise a hand and cover their eyes. For a few seconds a room full of adults sits like children playing hide and seek. And under the hands, six Hebrew words. Some children learn it as their first prayer, at bedtime, and tradition hopes it will be among the last words a person says in this life. Six words, said at the beginning and the end. Today: the sentence under the hand.
screen: `A HAND OVER THE EYES.` → `SIX HEBREW WORDS.` → `THE FIRST PRAYER AND THE LAST.`

segments.voice: The six words are: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad. "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." They come from the Torah, from the same passage that's rolled up inside the mezuzah, and the prayer is named for its first word. Shema. Hear. But the Hebrew verb is bigger than hearing with your ears. It means listen, pay attention, understand, even take it to heart and act on it. It's not here is a fact. It's are you listening? Notice who it's said to. Not to God. To Israel, to the people, to the person saying it. It's a sentence you say to yourself, out loud, to wake yourself up. A detail about the name. The word written there is God's four-letter name, which Jewish tradition doesn't pronounce. Reading aloud, people say Adonai, my Lord, instead. And a detail about the page. In a handwritten Torah scroll, two letters in this verse are written extra large: the last letter of the first word and the last letter of the last word. Together they spell ed, the Hebrew word for witness. Saying it, some teachers say, is a kind of testimony. Why the hand over the eyes? An old story remembers that Rabbi Judah the Prince, whom tradition credits with gathering the rabbis' early teachings into one book, passed his hand over his eyes when he said it. People still do: shut out everything you can see, just for a moment, so you can hear. The same passage says to speak these words when you lie down and when you rise up. So it's said morning and night, at bedtime, and at the end.
screen: `SHEMA — HEAR, LISTEN, TAKE IT IN.` · `SAID TO ISRAEL, NOT TO GOD.` · `TWO BIG LETTERS SPELL WITNESS.` · `A HAND OVER THE EYES, TO HEAR.` · then, large: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Cover your eyes with one hand, the way people do for the Shema. Let the room disappear. Breathe slowly and just listen, to whatever sound is left: a fan, traffic, your own breath. If you pray, you can say the six words on the way out. If not, let the breath out and simply hear.
The Shema. Six words that begin hear, O Israel, said morning and night with the eyes covered. Thirteenth word.
Your line: hear. Not only with the ears: listen, and take it in. Day thirteen.

14.title: intention
14.hook: intention; the difference between saying and meaning
14.howItsDone: Jews pray fixed prayers three times a day and try to say them with kavanah; many pause before praying to focus, and the silent standing prayer, the Amidah, is said with moving lips and no sound, as Hannah prayed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Shema, six words said with the eyes covered. Your line was hear. Day fourteen, the end of week two.

Someone drives home and pulls into the driveway without remembering a single turn. Someone reads a whole page, reaches the bottom, and has no idea what it said. Someone says love you at the end of a phone call the way they'd say bye. The mouth did the job. Nobody was there. Now imagine a tradition with words it says every day, morning and night, for a lifetime. The danger isn't forgetting them. It's saying them perfectly while you're somewhere else entirely. Judaism has a word for what's missing. Today: intention.
screen: `HOME, AND NO MEMORY OF THE DRIVE.` → `THE MOUTH DID THE JOB.` → `NOBODY WAS THERE.`

segments.voice: Kavanah comes from a root that means to aim, to direct, to point something at a target. Intention is aiming your heart where your words are going. The rabbis, discussing the Shema from yesterday, said that if a person directed their heart while reading it, they had done what was asked. They also remembered that the early pious ones would wait an hour before praying, just to direct their hearts. An hour of aiming, for a few minutes of prayer. The Bible's clearest picture of kavanah is a woman named Hannah, praying at the sanctuary for a child. She speaks in her heart; only her lips move, and no sound comes out. The priest thinks she's drunk. She isn't. She's praying as hard as anyone ever has, and the rabbis learned much of how to pray from her. One old line puts it simply: the Merciful One wants the heart. Then the honest part. The rabbis argued about whether a commandment done without intention still counts, and the discussion went on for centuries. Many say yes, the act counts, but it isn't the whole thing. And one teaching holds both sides together: do the good thing even when your heart isn't in it, because from doing it without the right intention, you come to do it with the right one. That's day ten again, do first, with a promise attached. This week you met Abraham, Jacob, Sinai, Shabbat, shalom, the Shema, and now the thing that makes any of them more than motions.
screen: `KAVANAH — TO AIM THE HEART.` · `AN HOUR OF AIMING FIRST.` · `HANNAH'S LIPS MOVE, NO SOUND.` · `DOING LEADS TO MEANING.` · then, large: `THE MERCIFUL ONE WANTS THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Pick one short thing you say every day without thinking: thank you, good morning, love you, or, if you pray, the Shema. For the first part of the sit, just aim: who is it for, and what do you actually mean by it? Then say it once, slowly, meaning every word.

original.note: Hebrew: intention, from a root meaning to aim or direct.
